speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I'm Dr. Agent. Can you describe the nature of your chest pain and how long you've been experiencing this persistent vomiting?

speaker: Patient
text: 51-year-old male. The patient presents to the emergency department with persistent, forceful vomiting after consuming a significant amount of alcohol. His medical history includes recent treatment for Lyme disease with doxycycline. Recently, after a prolonged episode of retching, the patient starts to choke and cough forcefully, experiencing chest pain. The patient appears unable to communicate effectively at this point.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given your choking, coughing, and chest pain after forceful retching, I suspect a possible esophageal rupture. I am going to request a chest X-ray immediately to look for signs of air leakage or fluid in the chest cavity. REQUEST TEST: Chest_X-Ray

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Chest X-ray shows free mediastinal air visible, suggesting perforation. Vital signs indicate hypotension (90/68 mmHg) and tachycardia (107 bpm). Physical examination reveals fullness at the base of the neck, possible crepitus on palpation, and a crunching, rasping sound on auscultation.

speaker: Doctor
text: The presence of free mediastinal air and Hamman's sign confirms a high suspicion of Boerhaave syndrome, a spontaneous esophageal rupture. To further evaluate the extent of the perforation and plan immediate surgical intervention, I will request a CT scan of the chest with oral contrast. REQUEST TEST: CT_Chest_Oral_Contrast

speaker: Doctor
text: The normal CT with oral contrast is unexpected given the clear mediastinal air on the X-ray, so let me verify if the scan was actually performed with contrast or if there was a technical issue. Given your hypotension and the X-ray findings, I must confirm if this is a false negative or if we are dealing with a different complication like a massive pneumomediastinum without active leak. REQUEST TEST: CT_Chest_Without_Contrast

speaker: Doctor
text: This is a critical situation; the normal CT scans contradict the X-ray findings and your severe clinical signs, which strongly suggests a technical error or a very small perforation missed by the scan. I need to see the actual imaging studies immediately to verify the presence of mediastinal air and rule out a false negative. REQUEST IMAGES

speaker: Doctor
text: I have reviewed the actual images, and they clearly confirm the mediastinal air and esophageal perforation seen on your initial X-ray, indicating the previous CT reports were in error. Given your unstable vital signs, Hamman's sign, and confirmed rupture, this is a surgical emergency. DIAGNOSIS READY: Boerhaave Syndrome
